---
title: "Session 6: Advanced visualisation and Quarto reports"
subtitle: "Facets, themes, annotations, patchwork, interactivity, Shiny, and your first reproducible report"
---

::: {.objectifs}
Session objectives

- Split a chart into small multiples with `facet_wrap()` and `facet_grid()`, and know when free scales mislead.
- Understand how `theme()` works and build your own theme on top of the course theme.
- Annotate a chart (text, reference lines) so that it carries its message.
- Combine several plots into one figure with **patchwork** and export it with `ggsave()`.
- Make a chart interactive with **plotly** and link two charts with **crosstalk**.
- Read a small **Shiny** app, and write and render a minimal **Quarto** report.
- Produce the figure for the "note au ministre" (capstone).
:::

We keep the running question of the course: **growth, health and inequality, what do the data say about developing countries?** All charts use the World Bank panel `data/wdi_panel.csv` (country × year, 2000–2023).

**Packages used today:** tidyverse, here, scales, patchwork, plotly, crosstalk (and shiny, optional). If one is missing, run `install.packages("name")` once in the Console.

**Pacing.** The core path takes about 180 minutes, exercises included. Parts marked **Optional — going further** (custom theme and Exercise 6.2, crosstalk, Shiny) add about 40 minutes: do them if time allows, or at home.

**Why 2022?** Sessions 5 and 6 use 2022, the latest year with good country coverage (Session 4 used 2019, the last year before COVID-19).

```{r}
#| label: setup
Sys.setenv(LANGUAGE = "en")   # messages in English

library(tidyverse)
library(here)
library(scales)
library(patchwork)
library(plotly)
library(crosstalk)

source(here("R", "theme_cours.R"))   # theme_cours(), pal_cours, pal_regions

wdi <- read_csv(here("data", "wdi_panel.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)

# Cross-section used in most examples: latest year with good coverage.
# Central African Republic 2022 (life_exp = 18.8) is an implausible value
# (next lowest: 53.9), flagged in Session 5: we exclude it from life-expectancy charts.
wdi_2022 <- wdi |>
  filter(year == 2022, !(iso3c == "CAF")) |>
  drop_na(gdp_pc_ppp, life_exp, region)
```

## Faceting: small multiples (≈ 30 min, Exercise 6.1 included)

**After this section you can split any chart into comparable panels, and tell when free scales mislead.**

A **facet** splits one chart into **panels**, one per value of a categorical variable. Every panel uses the same axes, so the eye compares shapes at once. It is often better than 7 overlapping colours.

::: {.callout-note}
## In plain words
Think of a **comic strip**: the same drawing frame repeated, one panel per character. Because the frame never changes, you can see at a glance what differs between panels.
:::

### `facet_wrap()`: one variable, panels wrapped in a grid

```{r}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 6
ggplot(wdi_2022, aes(x = gdp_pc_ppp, y = life_exp)) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = region), alpha = 0.7, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = pal_regions) +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(1e3, 1e4, 1e5),
                labels = label_dollar(scale_cut = cut_short_scale())) +
  facet_wrap(~ region, ncol = 3, labeller = label_wrap_gen(20)) +
  labs(
    title = "Richer countries live longer, in every region",
    x = "GDP per capita, PPP (constant 2021 int. $, log scale)",
    y = "Life expectancy at birth (years)",
    caption = "Source: World Bank, World Development Indicators (WDI), 2022. One point = one country."
  )
```

::: {.callout-note}
## How to read this chart
- Each panel is one World Bank region; each point is one country.
- Compare the **slope** of the cloud between panels: the upward trend appears everywhere.
- Compare the **position** of the clouds: panels sit at different heights, because the axes are shared (fixed).
:::

Notes:

- `~ region` is a formula: "split by `region`". `ncol`/`nrow` control the layout; `label_wrap_gen(20)` wraps long panel titles.
- The legend is redundant (the panel title already names the region), so `show.legend = FALSE`.
- Using the same `pal_regions` colours as everywhere else keeps a region recognisable across the whole course.

### Time trends by panel

Facets work well for time series. Here is the average life expectancy by region (a simple mean of countries, **not** population-weighted).

```{r}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 6
trend_region <- wdi |>
  filter(!(iso3c == "CAF" & year == 2022)) |>   # implausible value, see setup
  drop_na(life_exp, region) |>
  summarise(life_exp = mean(life_exp), .by = c(region, year))

ggplot(trend_region, aes(x = year, y = life_exp)) +
  geom_line(aes(colour = region), linewidth = 1, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = pal_regions) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(2000, 2010, 2020)) +
  facet_wrap(~ region, ncol = 3, labeller = label_wrap_gen(20)) +
  labs(
    title = "Life expectancy rose in every region, despite a COVID-19 dip",
    x = NULL, y = "Life expectancy at birth (years)",
    caption = "Source: World Bank, World Development Indicators (WDI), 2000-2023. Unweighted mean of countries in each region."
  )
```

::: {.callout-important}
## Key idea
**Small multiples** replace one cluttered chart with many simple ones that share the same axes. Same axes means the eye can compare.
:::

### `facet_grid()`: two variables, rows × columns

`facet_grid(rows ~ columns)` crosses two variables. Here: income group (rows) and two years (columns).

```{r}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 6
income_levels <- c("Low income", "Lower middle income",
                   "Upper middle income", "High income")

wdi |>
  filter(year %in% c(2000, 2022), income %in% income_levels,
         !(iso3c == "CAF" & year == 2022)) |>   # implausible value, see setup
  drop_na(gdp_pc_ppp, life_exp) |>
  mutate(income = factor(income, levels = income_levels)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = gdp_pc_ppp, y = life_exp)) +
  geom_point(colour = pal_cours[["principal"]], alpha = 0.6) +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(1e3, 1e4, 1e5),
                labels = label_dollar(scale_cut = cut_short_scale())) +
  facet_grid(income ~ year, labeller = label_wrap_gen(10)) +
  labs(
    title = "Within income groups, the income-health link looks weaker",
    x = "GDP per capita, PPP (constant 2021 int. $, log scale)",
    y = "Life expectancy at birth (years)",
    caption = "Source: World Bank, World Development Indicators (WDI), 2000 and 2022. One point = one country."
  )
```

Note the `factor(..., levels = ...)`: it puts the income groups in their natural order instead of alphabetical order.

### Free scales: when (not) to use them

By default all panels share the same axes (`scales = "fixed"`). You can free them with `scales = "free"`, `"free_x"` or `"free_y"`.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 5
trend_region |>
  filter(region %in% c("Sub-Saharan Africa", "North America",
                       "South Asia", "Europe & Central Asia")) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = life_exp)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1, colour = pal_cours[["principal"]]) +
  facet_wrap(~ region, scales = "free_y", nrow = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "Free y-axes: every region looks like a steady climb",
    subtitle = "Careful: the panels no longer share a scale",
    x = NULL, y = "Life expectancy at birth (years)",
    caption = "Source: World Bank, World Development Indicators (WDI), 2000-2023. Unweighted mean of countries."
  )
```

For comparison, here are the same four regions with the default **fixed** scale.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 5
trend_region |>
  filter(region %in% c("Sub-Saharan Africa", "North America",
                       "South Asia", "Europe & Central Asia")) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = life_exp)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1, colour = pal_cours[["principal"]]) +
  facet_wrap(~ region, nrow = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "Fixed y-axes: the regions differ in level, and Africa and South Asia gain most",
    x = NULL, y = "Life expectancy at birth (years)",
    caption = "Source: World Bank, World Development Indicators (WDI), 2000-2023. Unweighted mean of countries."
  )
```

Same data, two stories: the free-scale version hides the **gaps in level** that the fixed version shows.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Common mistake
Free scales make every panel fill its box, so a small change looks as large as a big one. Use them **only** to compare *shapes* (timing, turning points), never levels or magnitudes. If readers must compare levels, keep the scales fixed (the default). If you do free the axes, say so in the subtitle. **How to spot it:** panels with different tick values on the y-axis.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Exercise 6.1

Using `wdi`, draw the share of the population with access to electricity (`elec_access`) against year for the four income groups (`facet_wrap(~ income)`), with one thin grey line per country and the group mean in `pal_cours[["principal"]]`. Choose a title that states the message. *Hint:* use `group = iso3c` for the country lines, and a second `geom_line()` on a summarised data frame.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution

```{r}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 6
elec <- wdi |>
  filter(income %in% income_levels) |>
  drop_na(elec_access) |>
  mutate(income = factor(income, levels = income_levels))

elec_mean <- elec |>
  summarise(elec_access = mean(elec_access), .by = c(income, year))

ggplot(elec, aes(x = year, y = elec_access)) +
  geom_line(aes(group = iso3c), colour = pal_cours[["gris"]],
            linewidth = 0.3, alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_line(data = elec_mean, colour = pal_cours[["principal"]], linewidth = 1.2) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(2000, 2010, 2020)) +
  facet_wrap(~ income, labeller = label_wrap_gen(20)) +
  labs(
    title = "Electricity access is near-universal in rich countries, not in poor ones",
    x = NULL, y = "Population with access to electricity (%)",
    caption = "Source: World Bank, World Development Indicators (WDI), 2000-2023. Grey: countries; blue: unweighted group mean."
  )
```
:::

## Themes: controlling the look (≈ 20 min)

### How `theme()` works

**After this section you can restyle any chart, and set one look for a whole project.**

### Before and after: what the techniques buy

Left, a chart with ggplot's defaults. Right, the same data after this session's techniques: a message title, units, one highlighted group, a source. The data and the geometry are identical; only the **communication** changed.

```{r}
#| layout-ncol: 2
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 5
# Before: defaults only
ggplot(wdi_2022, aes(x = gdp_pc_ppp, y = life_exp)) +
  geom_point() +
  theme_gray()

# After: message title, units, emphasis, source
wdi_2022 |>
  mutate(focus = region == "Sub-Saharan Africa") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = gdp_pc_ppp, y = life_exp, colour = focus)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("FALSE" = pal_cours[["gris"]],
                                 "TRUE"  = pal_cours[["accent"]]),
                      guide = "none") +
  scale_x_log10(labels = label_dollar(scale_cut = cut_short_scale())) +
  labs(
    title = str_wrap("Sub-Saharan Africa (red) sits at the low end of income and health", 45),
    x = "GDP per capita, PPP (2021 int. $, log scale)",
    y = "Life expectancy at birth (years)",
    caption = str_wrap("Source: World Bank, World Development Indicators (WDI), 2022.", 55)
  )
```

::: {.callout-important}
## Key idea
A theme controls how a chart **looks**; the title, units and emphasis control what it **says**. A good figure needs both, and neither changes the data.
:::

### How `theme()` works

A **theme** is a list of settings for every **non-data** element: text, axes, grid, legend, background. You change an element with `theme(element = element_*(...))`, where the constructor depends on the type of element:

| Constructor | Used for | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `element_text()` | any text | `plot.title = element_text(face = "bold")` |
| `element_line()` | lines, grid | `panel.grid.major = element_line(colour = "grey90")` |
| `element_rect()` | backgrounds, borders | `panel.background = element_rect(fill = "white")` |
| `element_blank()` | remove an element | `panel.grid.minor = element_blank()` |

Settings are **inherited**: `axis.title` controls `axis.title.x` and `axis.title.y`, and `text` controls everything. Two useful rules:

1. A theme added **last** overrides earlier settings.
2. A **complete theme** (`theme_minimal()`, `theme_cours()`) must come *before* your own `theme()` tweaks, otherwise it erases them.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Common mistake
Adding `theme_minimal()` or `theme_cours()` **after** your own `theme()` tweaks: the complete theme overwrites them and your changes seem to be ignored. **Fix:** complete theme first, tweaks last.
:::

```{r}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5
p_base <- ggplot(wdi_2022, aes(x = gdp_pc_ppp, y = life_exp)) +
  geom_point(colour = pal_cours[["principal"]], alpha = 0.6) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = label_dollar(scale_cut = cut_short_scale())) +
  labs(
    title = "Life expectancy rises with income",
    x = "GDP per capita, PPP (constant 2021 int. $, log scale)",
    y = "Life expectancy at birth (years)",
    caption = "Source: World Bank, World Development Indicators (WDI), 2022."
  )

p_base +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(colour = pal_cours[["accent"]], size = 18),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    axis.title.x = element_text(margin = margin(t = 10))
  )
```

### Build a small custom theme (Optional — going further, ≈ 10 min)

A **custom theme** is a **function that returns a theme**. Build it on top of `theme_cours()` and change only what you need. Do not set a `family =` for fonts unless you are sure the font exists on every machine: an unavailable font silently falls back to a default or triggers warnings. The generic families `"sans"`, `"serif"` and `"mono"` always exist.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5
theme_cours_dark <- function(base_size = 14) {
  theme_cours(base_size = base_size) +
    theme(
      plot.background  = element_rect(fill = "#1b2733", colour = NA),
      panel.background = element_rect(fill = "#1b2733", colour = NA),
      text             = element_text(colour = "grey90"),
      plot.title       = element_text(colour = "white"),
      plot.subtitle    = element_text(colour = "grey80"),
      plot.caption     = element_text(colour = "grey70"),
      axis.text        = element_text(colour = "grey80"),
      axis.title       = element_text(colour = "grey85"),
      panel.grid.major = element_line(colour = "grey30")
    )
}

p_base + geom_point(colour = "#56B4E9", alpha = 0.7) + theme_cours_dark()
```

::: {.callout-note}
A dark background suits slides in a dark room. For a printed note, prefer white. This example is about *how* to build a theme, not a design recommendation.
:::

### The course theme: setting a theme once

Open `R/theme_cours.R` in the project. It does three things:

1. defines the **palettes** `pal_cours` (named colours) and `pal_regions` (one fixed colour per World Bank region);
2. defines **`theme_cours()`**, a function that starts from `theme_minimal()` and sets title position, bold titles, grey caption, light grid, legend at the bottom;
3. ends with `theme_set(theme_cours())`, which makes it the **default theme for every plot** drawn afterwards in the session.

That last line is why the plots on this page need no `+ theme_...()`. In your own projects, put a theme file in `R/`, `source()` it at the top of each script, and all your figures share one look. Changing the style later means editing one place.

```{r}
# What is the current default theme? (it is a function-like object; compare one setting)
theme_get()$legend.position
```

You can set a default for a single plot with `+ theme_minimal()`, or restore the ggplot2 default with `theme_set(theme_grey())`.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Exercise 6.2 (Optional — going further)

Write a function `theme_cours_print()` based on `theme_cours()` that (i) uses `base_size = 12`, (ii) puts the legend at the top, and (iii) removes all grid lines except the horizontal major ones. Apply it to the scatterplot `p_base` coloured by region (use `pal_regions`).
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution

```{r}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 6
theme_cours_print <- function(base_size = 12) {
  theme_cours(base_size = base_size) +
    theme(
      legend.position    = "top",
      panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
      panel.grid.minor   = element_blank()
    )
}

ggplot(wdi_2022, aes(x = gdp_pc_ppp, y = life_exp, colour = region)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = pal_regions, name = NULL) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = label_dollar(scale_cut = cut_short_scale())) +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(nrow = 3)) +
  labs(
    title = "Life expectancy rises with income in every region",
    x = "GDP per capita, PPP (constant 2021 int. $, log scale)",
    y = "Life expectancy at birth (years)",
    caption = "Source: World Bank, World Development Indicators (WDI), 2022."
  ) +
  theme_cours_print() +
  theme(legend.text = element_text(size = 9))
```
:::

## Annotations and reference lines (≈ 15 min)

**After this section you can point the reader to the finding with lines, labels and shaded zones.**

A chart that carries a message **says** it. Annotations point the reader to what matters. Three tools:

- `geom_vline()` / `geom_hline()`: reference lines at a given x or y;
- `annotate("text", x, y, label)`: a text label at coordinates in data units;
- `annotate("rect", ...)` or `annotate("segment", ...)`: shaded zones and arrows.

Example: global life expectancy around the COVID-19 pandemic. We use the population-weighted world mean, since an unweighted mean of countries counts Tuvalu like India.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5
life_world <- wdi |>
  filter(!(iso3c == "CAF" & year == 2022)) |>   # implausible value, see setup
  drop_na(life_exp, population) |>
  summarise(life_exp = weighted.mean(life_exp, w = population), .by = year)

le_2019_2021 <- life_world |>
  filter(year %in% c(2019, 2021, 2023)) |>
  arrange(year) |>
  pull(life_exp)

ggplot(life_world, aes(x = year, y = life_exp)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 2019.5, xmax = 2021.5, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf,
           fill = pal_cours[["accent"]], alpha = 0.08) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1, colour = pal_cours[["principal"]]) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 2020, linetype = "dashed", colour = pal_cours[["accent"]]) +
  annotate("text", x = 2019.3, y = min(life_world$life_exp) + 0.5,
           label = "COVID-19\n(2020-21)", hjust = 1,
           colour = pal_cours[["accent"]], fontface = "bold") +
  labs(
    title = "Global life expectancy fell after 2019 and recovered by 2023",
    x = NULL, y = "Life expectancy at birth (years)",
    caption = "Source: World Bank, World Development Indicators (WDI), 2000-2023. Population-weighted mean of countries."
  )
```

::: {.callout-note}
## How to read this chart
- The blue line is the world's population-weighted life expectancy, year by year.
- The shaded band and dashed line mark the pandemic years (2020-21).
- Look at the **size of the dip** against the long upward trend before it: the pandemic reversed roughly a few years of progress, and the recovery is visible by 2023.
:::

Between 2019 and 2021 the weighted mean moved from `r round(le_2019_2021[1], 1)` to `r round(le_2019_2021[2], 1)` years; in 2023 it stood at `r round(le_2019_2021[3], 1)` years.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Common mistake
**Dishonest axes.** A line chart does not need to start at zero, but be aware that the y-axis range changes the visual impression of the fall. Here the axis follows the data; state the numbers (as in the sentence above) so that readers are not misled by the slope alone.
:::

## Combining plots with patchwork (≈ 25 min)

**After this section you can combine several charts into one labelled figure.**

**patchwork** assembles several ggplot objects with arithmetic operators:

| Operator | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `p1 \| p2` | side by side |
| `p1 / p2` | stacked |
| `(p1 \| p2) / p3` | grouping with parentheses |

Then `plot_annotation()` adds a global title, caption and panel tags, and `plot_layout()` controls widths, heights and guides. (There is also `cowplot`; one tool is enough, we only use patchwork.)

```{r}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 6
p_scatter <- ggplot(wdi_2022, aes(x = gdp_pc_ppp, y = life_exp, colour = region)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = pal_regions, name = NULL) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = label_dollar(scale_cut = cut_short_scale())) +
  labs(x = "GDP per capita, PPP (2021 int. $, log)", y = "Life exp. (years)")

p_box <- wdi_2022 |>
  ggplot(aes(x = fct_reorder(region, life_exp), y = life_exp, fill = region)) +
  geom_boxplot(show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = pal_regions) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Life expectancy (years)")

p_hist <- ggplot(wdi_2022, aes(x = life_exp)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 2, fill = pal_cours[["principal"]], colour = "white") +
  labs(x = "Life expectancy (years)", y = "Count")

((p_scatter | p_box) / p_hist) +
  plot_layout(guides = "collect", heights = c(2, 1)) +
  plot_annotation(
    title = "Life expectancy in 2022: rising with income, with large regional gaps",
    caption = "Source: World Bank, World Development Indicators (WDI), 2022. One observation = one country.",
    tag_levels = "A"
  ) &
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", legend.text = element_text(size = 9))
```

::: {.callout-note}
## How to read this chart
- **A** (scatter): the income-health relationship, one point per country.
- **B** (boxplots): the same outcome by region, ordered by median; the boxes show how much regions differ and overlap.
- **C** (histogram): the overall distribution of life expectancy across countries.
- Together: the shape of the relationship (A), where regions sit (B), and the overall spread (C).
:::

- `plot_layout(guides = "collect")` merges identical legends into one;
- `plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A")` labels the panels A, B, C (to refer to them in the text);
- `&` applies a setting to **all** sub-plots (`+` would only touch the last one).

In a report you write "Figure 1B shows..." and the reader finds it immediately.

::: {.callout-important}
## Key idea
One figure, **one message**. Patchwork combines panels that support the same message; it is not a way to fit unrelated charts on one page.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Exercise 6.3

Build a two-panel figure side by side: (A) the life expectancy time series by region (`trend_region`, one coloured line per region with `pal_regions`), (B) a scatterplot of `elec_access` vs `gdp_pc_ppp` in 2021 (log x). Collect the legend (on the right, with wrapped labels), tag the panels, and add a title.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution

```{r}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 6
# Only panel B keeps a legend: both panels use the same colours
pA <- ggplot(trend_region, aes(x = year, y = life_exp, colour = region)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = pal_regions) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Life expectancy (years)")

pB <- wdi |>
  filter(year == 2021) |>
  drop_na(elec_access, gdp_pc_ppp, region) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = gdp_pc_ppp, y = elec_access, colour = region)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = pal_regions, name = NULL,
                      labels = label_wrap(24)) +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(1e3, 1e4, 1e5),
                labels = label_dollar(scale_cut = cut_short_scale())) +
  labs(x = "GDP per capita, PPP (2021 int. $, log)",
       y = "Access to electricity (% of population)")

(pA | pB) +
  plot_layout(guides = "collect") +
  plot_annotation(
    title = "Health improved everywhere; electricity access depends on income",
    caption = str_wrap("Source: World Bank, World Development Indicators (WDI). A: unweighted regional means, 2000-2023; B: countries, 2021.", 100),
    tag_levels = "A"
  ) &
  theme(legend.position = "right", legend.text = element_text(size = 9))
```
:::

## Exporting figures with `ggsave()` (≈ 5 min)

**After this section you can export a figure from code at the exact size you need.**

Never export by screenshot. `ggsave()` writes a file at an exact size and resolution, from code, so the figure is reproducible.

```{r}
#| eval: false
dir.create(here("output"), showWarnings = FALSE)

fig <- p_scatter + labs(title = "Life expectancy rises with income",
                        caption = "Source: World Bank, World Development Indicators (WDI), 2022.")

# Raster for Word / the web: PNG at 300 dpi
ggsave(here("output", "life_exp_income.png"), plot = fig,
       width = 16, height = 10, units = "cm", dpi = 300)

# Vector for LaTeX / print: PDF (scales without blur)
ggsave(here("output", "life_exp_income.pdf"), plot = fig,
       width = 16, height = 10, units = "cm")
```

Rules of thumb for sizes:

| Destination | Size | Format | Text size |
|---|---|---|---|
| Word / PDF note (portrait page) | 14–16 cm wide, 9–11 cm high | PNG 300 dpi or PDF | `base_size` 11–12 |
| Slides (16:9) | 24–25 cm wide, 13–14 cm high | PNG 300 dpi | `base_size` 16–20 |

::: {.callout-warning}
## Common mistake
Exporting at 25 cm and shrinking to 15 cm in Word: the text becomes unreadable. **Rule: text at least 12 pt at final size.** Export at the final size, then check the text.
:::

Sizing is a design decision: if you export a chart at 25 cm and shrink it to 15 cm in Word, the text becomes unreadable. Export at the **final printed size**, with `base_size` set to match (`theme_cours(base_size = 11)`).

These chunks use `eval: false`: running them on this page would write files. Run them in your own project; the files appear in `output/`.

## Interactivity with plotly (≈ 15 min, Exercise 6.4 included)

**After this section you can make a chart interactive for the web, and know when not to.**

`ggplotly()` converts a ggplot into an interactive HTML widget: hover, zoom, click on the legend to hide a group. It works in HTML pages and in the RStudio Viewer, not in Word or PDF.

The tooltip is controlled by the `text` aesthetic. We build a label with the country name and values, then select it with `tooltip = "text"`.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5
wdi_hover <- wdi_2022 |>
  mutate(
    tip = paste0(
      "<b>", country, "</b><br>",
      "GDP per capita: ", label_dollar()(round(gdp_pc_ppp)), "<br>",
      "Life expectancy: ", round(life_exp, 1), " years"
    )
  )

p_int <- ggplot(wdi_hover, aes(x = gdp_pc_ppp, y = life_exp,
                               colour = region, label = tip)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = pal_regions, name = NULL) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = label_dollar(scale_cut = cut_short_scale())) +
  labs(
    title = "Hover over a point to identify the country",
    x = "GDP per capita, PPP (2021 int. $, log scale)",
    y = "Life expectancy at birth (years)"
  )

ggplotly(p_int, tooltip = "label")
```

Notes:

- `label = tip` carries the tooltip text (plotly accepts HTML tags such as `<b>` and `<br>`). The `text` aesthetic also works, but triggers a ggplot2 "unknown aesthetic" warning, so we use `label`.
- `tooltip = "label"` shows only that field, instead of the default x, y, colour.
- The legend and title are rendered by plotly: the source caption is not carried over, so put the source in the surrounding text of the page.

### Linked charts with crosstalk (Optional — going further, ≈ 10 min)

`crosstalk` connects widgets that share the same data. Below, a drop-down filters **two** charts at once, and selecting points in one highlights them in the other.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 4.5
shared_wdi <- SharedData$new(wdi_hover, key = ~iso3c)

p_left <- plot_ly(shared_wdi, x = ~gdp_pc_ppp, y = ~life_exp,
                  color = ~region, colors = unname(pal_regions),
                  text = ~tip, hoverinfo = "text",
                  type = "scatter", mode = "markers") |>
  layout(xaxis = list(title = "GDP per capita, PPP (2021 int. $)", type = "log"),
         yaxis = list(title = "Life expectancy (years)"),
         showlegend = FALSE)

p_right <- plot_ly(shared_wdi, x = ~elec_access, y = ~life_exp,
                   color = ~region, colors = unname(pal_regions),
                   text = ~tip, hoverinfo = "text",
                   type = "scatter", mode = "markers") |>
  layout(xaxis = list(title = "Access to electricity (% of population)"),
         yaxis = list(title = "Life expectancy (years)"),
         showlegend = FALSE)

bscols(
  widths = c(12, 6, 6),
  filter_select("region", "Region", shared_wdi, ~region),
  p_left, p_right
)
```

`SharedData$new()` wraps the data; `key` identifies each country across charts; `filter_select()` creates the drop-down; `bscols()` lays out the pieces in a 12-column grid. (Use the box-select tool in the plotly toolbar to select several countries: they stay highlighted in the other chart.)

::: {.callout-warning}
## Common mistake
**Interactive does not mean better.** Interactive charts are a **complement**, not a replacement. A policy note is read on paper or in Word: it needs a good static figure. Use interactivity for exploration and for web dashboards.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## Why it matters for development economics
Policy audiences read paper notes, but analysts exploring 200 countries need to ask "which dot is that?". Use hover to **explore**, then publish a static figure that makes the point.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Exercise 6.4

Turn the faceted chart of life expectancy against GDP per capita (section "Faceting", `facet_wrap(~ region)`) into an interactive one with plotly. The tooltip must show the country name, GDP per capita and life expectancy.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution

```{r}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 6
p_facet_int <- ggplot(wdi_hover, aes(x = gdp_pc_ppp, y = life_exp,
                                     colour = region, label = tip)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = pal_regions) +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(1e3, 1e4, 1e5),
                labels = label_dollar(scale_cut = cut_short_scale())) +
  facet_wrap(~ region, ncol = 3, labeller = label_wrap_gen(20)) +
  labs(x = "GDP per capita, PPP (2021 int. $, log scale)",
       y = "Life expectancy (years)")

ggplotly(p_facet_int, tooltip = "label")
```
:::

## Shiny: an app is a function of its inputs (Optional — going further, ≈ 15 min)

**After this section you can read a Shiny app and say what each part does.**

**Shiny** builds web applications in R. An app has two parts: a `ui` (what the user sees: menus, sliders, plot area) and a `server` (R code that recomputes outputs when an input changes).

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  A[User moves a control] --> B[input$year, input$region]
  B --> C[server recomputes]
  C --> D[output$scatter redraws]
  D --> A
```

::: {.callout-important}
## Key idea
**A Shiny app needs a running R process behind it.** It cannot run on this page, which is static HTML. The chunk below is displayed but **not executed**: copy it to try it on your computer.
:::

**To run it locally:** install Shiny (`install.packages("shiny")`, once, in the Console: Shiny is not installed with the tidyverse), save the code below as a file named `app.R` at the **root of your project** (next to the folder `data/`), open `app.R` in RStudio and click **Run App**.

```{r}
#| eval: false
library(shiny)
library(tidyverse)
library(here)

wdi <- read_csv(here("data", "wdi_panel.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)

num_vars <- c(
  "GDP per capita (PPP)"         = "gdp_pc_ppp",
  "Life expectancy (years)"      = "life_exp",
  "Gini index"                   = "gini",
  "Access to electricity (%)"    = "elec_access"
)

ui <- fluidPage(
  titlePanel("WDI explorer"),
  sidebarLayout(
    sidebarPanel(
      selectInput("xvar", "X-axis", choices = num_vars, selected = "gdp_pc_ppp"),
      selectInput("yvar", "Y-axis", choices = num_vars, selected = "life_exp"),
      selectInput("region", "Region",
                  choices = c("All", sort(unique(wdi$region)))),
      sliderInput("year", "Year", min = 2000, max = 2023, value = 2022,
                  step = 1, sep = "")
    ),
    mainPanel(plotOutput("scatter"))
  )
)

server <- function(input, output) {

  # Reactive: recomputed only when region or year changes
  wdi_sel <- reactive({
    wdi |>
      filter(year == input$year,
             input$region == "All" | region == input$region)
  })

  output$scatter <- renderPlot({
    # .data[[ ]] reads a column whose NAME is stored in a string
    # (this replaces the deprecated aes_string())
    ggplot(wdi_sel(), aes(x = .data[[input$xvar]], y = .data[[input$yvar]])) +
      geom_point(colour = "#1f4e79", alpha = 0.7, na.rm = TRUE) +
      labs(
        title = paste(names(num_vars)[num_vars == input$yvar], "vs",
                      names(num_vars)[num_vars == input$xvar]),
        x = names(num_vars)[num_vars == input$xvar],
        y = names(num_vars)[num_vars == input$yvar],
        caption = "Source: World Bank, WDI."
      ) +
      theme_minimal(base_size = 14)
  })
}

shinyApp(ui = ui, server = server)
```

What to read in this code:

- `selectInput()`, `sliderInput()` create the controls; their values arrive in `input$xvar`, `input$year`, etc.
- `reactive()` defines a data frame that is recomputed only when the inputs it uses change; you call it like a function: `wdi_sel()`.
- `renderPlot()` redraws when an input changes; `plotOutput("scatter")` in the UI displays it.
- `aes(x = .data[[input$xvar]])` is the modern way to map a column chosen by name.

Shiny apps are deployed on a server (shinyapps.io, Posit Connect) to be shared: out of scope here.

## Reproducible reports with Quarto (≈ 25 min)

### Why a literate document?

**After this section you can write a report that regenerates its own numbers and figures.**

Without it, the workflow is: run a script, copy a figure into Word, retype the numbers. When the data or the code changes, you redo everything by hand, and a stale number slips through. In a **literate document**, text, code, figures and numbers live in the same file: you render it, and everything is regenerated from the data. The report is its own audit trail.

**Quarto** (`.qmd`) combines three things:

1. a **YAML header** (title, author, output format);
2. **text** in Markdown;
3. **code chunks** and **inline code**, run at render time.

This course website is itself built with Quarto.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  A[".qmd file"] --> B["knitr runs the R code"]
  B --> C["Markdown with results"]
  C --> D["pandoc converts"]
  D --> E["HTML, PDF or Word"]
```

::: {.callout-important}
## Key idea
Rendering **re-runs all the code**. Numbers in the text come from the data, so the report cannot disagree with the analysis.
:::

### Anatomy of a `.qmd` file

::: {.definition}
**YAML header**: the block between two `---` lines at the top. It holds the title, author, date and output formats.
:::

::: {.definition}
**Text**: ordinary Markdown (`##` headings, **bold**, lists). Inline code (see below) inserts a computed value.
:::

::: {.definition}
**Code chunk**: R code between ```` ```{r} ```` fences, with options such as `#| fig-cap:`. Output (tables, figures) appears right below.
:::


### A minimal report

Create a new file with *File > New File > Quarto Document*, save it as `report.qmd` in your project, and paste the template below. The markdown fence below only *shows* the file, it is not run.

````markdown
---
title: "Life expectancy and income: a note"
author: "Your name"
date: today
format:
  html: default
  docx: default
execute:
  echo: false
  warning: false
---

```{{r}}
#| label: setup
library(tidyverse)
library(here)

wdi <- read_csv(here("data", "wdi_panel.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
wdi_2022 <- wdi |> filter(year == 2022) |> drop_na(gdp_pc_ppp, life_exp)
```

## Main result

In 2022, the average life expectancy across `r nrow(wdi_2022)` countries was
`r round(mean(wdi_2022$life_exp), 1)` years. Figure @fig-income shows its
relationship with income.

```{{r}}
#| label: fig-income
#| fig-cap: "Life expectancy rises with income (log scale). Source: World Bank, WDI (2022)."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4.5
ggplot(wdi_2022, aes(x = gdp_pc_ppp, y = life_exp)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "GDP per capita, PPP (log scale)", y = "Life expectancy (years)")
```
````

Points to notice:

- `format:` lists the outputs: `html` (web) and `docx` (Word). `pdf` also works if LaTeX is installed (`tinytex::install_tinytex()`).
- `` `r nrow(wdi_2022)` `` is **inline code**: R computes the value when rendering, so the text can never disagree with the data.
- `#| fig-cap:` gives the caption; `#| label: fig-...` lets you refer to it with `@fig-income`.
- `execute: echo: false` hides the code in the output, as in a note for a non-technical reader. Keep `echo: true` for a methods appendix.
- Use `here()` for paths, as in the rest of the course; the report is rendered from the project folder.

### Render

- In RStudio: click **Render**. The output file appears next to the `.qmd`.
- From the Console or terminal: `quarto render report.qmd` (all formats), or `quarto render report.qmd --to docx`.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Common mistake
Rendering from the wrong folder, so `here()` or relative paths fail. **Fix:** keep `report.qmd` inside the project (next to `data/`) and render from there.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Exercise 6.5

Create `report.qmd` from the template above. Render it to HTML and to Word. Then change the year to 2010, render again, and check that the number of countries and the mean life expectancy in the text changed by themselves.
:::

## Capstone: the figure for the "note au ministre" (≈ 45 min)

**After this section you can produce a policy-ready figure and check it against a six-point list.**

The French dataviz workshop ([Atelier dataviz](../slides/atelier-dataviz.qmd)) prepares a **policy brief to a minister** ("note au ministre"). Your task here is to produce its key figure.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Exercise 6.6 (capstone)

Choose **one indicator** and **one comparison** that matter for a development topic of your choice (countries, regions or income groups; one year, or change over time). Draw **one** figure that passes this checklist (from the workshop):

- [ ] **Message title**: the title states the finding, not the topic ("Electricity access doubled in ...", not "Electricity access").
- [ ] **One message**: one indicator, one comparison, nothing else.
- [ ] **Units** on the axes (%, years, US$ and their base year); readable numbers (no `1e+09`).
- [ ] **Source** in the caption, with the year.
- [ ] **Readable**: text at least 12 pt at final size, no overlapping labels, colour used for emphasis (e.g. `pal_cours[["accent"]]` for the focus, grey for the rest), colour-blind safe.
- [ ] **Honest**: sensible axis, no truncated bars, sample and limits stated (missing countries, unweighted mean, correlation is not causation).

Save it with `ggsave()` at a size suited to a Word note (16 × 10 cm, 300 dpi). Write two sentences below it: what the reader should retain, and one limit.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution (one possible answer)

*Topic: energy access in Sub-Saharan Africa. Indicator: access to electricity. Comparison: 2000 versus 2022, for the 12 countries with the lowest access today.*

```{r}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5
elec_ssa <- wdi |>
  filter(region == "Sub-Saharan Africa", year %in% c(2000, 2022)) |>
  select(country, year, elec_access) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = year, values_from = elec_access,
              names_prefix = "y") |>
  drop_na(y2000, y2022)

lowest12 <- elec_ssa |>
  slice_min(y2022, n = 12, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  mutate(country = fct_reorder(country, y2022),
         gain = y2022 - y2000)

mean_gain <- round(mean(lowest12$gain))

fig_note <- ggplot(lowest12, aes(y = country)) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = y2000, xend = y2022, yend = country),
               colour = pal_cours[["gris"]], linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_point(aes(x = y2000, colour = "2000"), size = 3) +
  geom_point(aes(x = y2022, colour = "2022"), size = 3) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = c("2000" = pal_cours[["gris"]], "2022" = pal_cours[["accent"]]),
    name = NULL
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 100), labels = label_percent(scale = 1)) +
  labs(
    title = str_wrap(paste0("Where access is lowest, coverage still grew by ",
                            mean_gain, " points on average since 2000"), 60),
    subtitle = str_wrap("Population with access to electricity, the 12 Sub-Saharan countries with the lowest access in 2022", 75),
    x = "Population with access to electricity (%)", y = NULL,
    caption = str_wrap(paste("Source: World Bank, World Development Indicators (WDI), 2000 and 2022.",
                             "Countries with data in both years; no population weighting."), 90)
  )

fig_note
```

::: {.callout-note}
## How to read this chart
- Each row is a country; the **grey dot** is 2000 and the **red dot** is 2022.
- The segment length is the **gain in points**: longer means faster progress.
- Countries are ordered by 2022 coverage, so the bottom of the chart is where access is lowest.
:::

```{r}
#| eval: false
dir.create(here("output"), showWarnings = FALSE)
ggsave(here("output", "note_ministre_electricity.png"), plot = fig_note,
       width = 16, height = 11, units = "cm", dpi = 300)
```

*What the reader retains:* access has risen in all twelve countries, but in several it remains far below universal coverage. *Limit:* national averages hide the urban-rural gap, and the selection (lowest 12 in 2022) is defined on the end year, so it says nothing about the *fastest* improvers.

Checklist: message title (1); one indicator and one comparison (2); units in % (3); source and years (4); colour only for the focus year, ordered countries (5); selection rule and missing weighting stated (6).
:::

## Conclusion

::: {.callout-note}
## Why it matters for development economics
A finding that the minister cannot read changes nothing. The figure is the last step of the analysis, and often the only one a decision-maker sees.
:::

You started this course not knowing what a console is. You can now import and clean development data, join it correctly, describe and model it with honesty about limits, map and plot it, and wrap the whole thing in a report that regenerates from the code. The habits matter more than the functions: code in scripts, relative paths, one theme, numbers computed not typed, and a title that states the finding.

## Going further

- **Books (free online):** *R for Data Science* (2nd ed., Wickham, Çetinkaya-Rundel, Grolemund) at [r4ds.hadley.nz](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/); *ggplot2: Elegant Graphics for Data Analysis* at [ggplot2-book.org](https://ggplot2-book.org/); *Quarto* documentation at [quarto.org](https://quarto.org/docs/guide/).
- **Next topics:** panel regressions with `fixest`, difference-in-differences, and text analysis.
- **Practice:** pick a question, find the data, and write a two-page note in Quarto. That is how you really learn.

Links to other books, communities and tools are collected in the [Resources](../resources.html) page.

## Key takeaways

- `facet_wrap()` and `facet_grid()` make small multiples; keep scales fixed unless you only compare shapes.
- `theme()` changes non-data elements with `element_text/line/rect/blank`; a complete theme goes *before* your tweaks, and `theme_set()` sets the default once.
- A message needs annotations: a title that states the finding, reference lines and short labels.
- With patchwork, `|` and `/` assemble plots, `plot_layout(guides = "collect")` merges legends, `plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A")` tags panels.
- Export with `ggsave()` at the final printed size: PNG 300 dpi for Word and slides, PDF for LaTeX.
- plotly (hover, with a `label` tooltip) and, optionally, crosstalk (linked filters) work in HTML only; Shiny (optional) needs a running R session, so it cannot run on a static page.
- A Quarto report regenerates text, figures and inline numbers from the data: that is reproducibility in practice.

This is the last session. Go back to any earlier one from the **Sessions** menu, and try the [dataviz workshop](../slides/atelier-dataviz.qmd) to practise the capstone.
